headline: imec told ECOC on Thursday that thinning an avalanche photodiode's multiplication layer below 100 nanometres buys 100 gigahertz of bandwidth at a 5-volt bias, and used it to receive 400 gigabits a second.

items.title: Thin the multiplication layer below 100 nm and the APD runs off 5 V
items.dek: imec told the ECOC optical-communications conference on Thursday that it has built a germanium-on-silicon avalanche photodiode — a detector that multiplies its own photocurrent before any amplifier sees it — with 100 gigahertz of bandwidth at a 5-volt bias.
items.why_it_matters: Multiplication inside the detector is receiver sensitivity you do not have to buy with laser power: imec puts the improvement at 3 dB. The usual price is a reverse bias of tens of volts, which needs its own supply rail and keeps the photodiode off the package that holds the transimpedance amplifier and the serialiser. Bringing the operating point down to a voltage ordinary CMOS already has removes that separation, and it does so without trading away speed — which is the part that normally breaks, because gain and bandwidth pull against each other in this class of device.
items.background_md: A conventional photodiode yields at most one electron per absorbed photon, so at hundreds of gigabits a second the photocurrent reaching the amplifier is small and the amplifier's own noise sets the weakest signal that can still be read. An avalanche photodiode inserts gain ahead of that noise: carriers are accelerated hard enough to ionise the lattice and free more carriers. Impact ionisation needs a very high field, the multiplication is a random process that adds excess noise, and the time carriers spend crossing the multiplying region caps how fast a high-gain device can be.
items.deeper_md:
The structure is a separate-absorption-charge-multiplication diode with the charge layer deleted and the multiplication region scaled below 100 nm, in a deeply recessed germanium-in-silicon geometry. Two consequences follow from the thickness alone. A shorter region reaches the ionisation field at a lower voltage, which is where 5 V comes from; and carriers cross it faster, so the transit-limited bandwidth goes up rather than collapsing as gain is added. imec reports 100 GHz, 1.8 A/W responsivity and roughly 2× internal gain in both the O- and C-bands on its 300 mm iSiPP300 line, paired on the transmit side with a beyond-110 GHz germanium electro-absorption modulator to make the link.

Compare the journal version of the same device family. In *Journal of Lightwave Technology* **44**(16) 6958, Shahin and co-workers report peak bandwidth above 100 GHz but **70 GHz at 2 A/W, at 7 V** reverse bias. Conference numbers are best-die numbers at a chosen operating point. imec's own stated next steps — reliability across temperature and optical input power, and integration with receiver electronics — are the two things that decide whether any of this survives in a module.

glossary.definition: The factor by which impact ionisation multiplies the photocurrent inside the diode; here about 2, applied before the amplifier so the amplifier's noise is divided by it.
Photocurrent out per watt of optical power in. It folds absorption efficiency and any internal gain into one number, which is why an APD can exceed what a gainless diode of the same material reaches.

The two wavelength windows silica fibre is used in — the shorter one where chromatic dispersion is near zero, which suits short datacentre links, and the longer one where attenuation is lowest, which suits reach.
A diode layout that puts photon absorption in one layer and carrier multiplication in another, with a doped charge layer between them shaping the field so each layer sees the field it needs.

items.fab_angle: The number that makes this device is a vertical dimension, not a printed one: a sub-100 nm multiplication region is set by a recess etch and a germanium epitaxy step and measured in cross-section, not by a mask. Deleting the charge layer also deletes an implant and its anneal from the flow, which is a thermal-budget saving in a photonics module that has transistors nearby.

items.title: Where the gate's charge sits turns out to be a design variable
items.dek: Researchers led by Hoon Hahn Yoon fluorinated the surface of bismuth selenide into an insulator and used the layered pair as a transistor gate stack; in the molybdenum-disulfide devices they gated that way, the drain voltage reaches through to the channel about seven times less than with the fluoride alone.
items.why_it_matters: Gate-stack engineering has spent twenty years hunting for thinner, higher-permittivity insulators on the assumption that the electrode behind them is a perfect equipotential surface. It is not — charge in a real gate sits a finite distance back from the interface, and that distance shows up as a capacitance in series with the dielectric. This work measures the penalty, finds the stack capacitance lower than the insulator on its own would predict, and still gets better electrostatic control of the channel. If both of those hold up, the position and compressibility of the gate's screening charge is a lever separate from oxide thickness, and nobody has been pulling it.
items.background_md: A transistor switches cleanly when the gate holds the channel potential against the drain, and the usual lever is gate capacitance per unit area: thin the insulator, raise its permittivity. Two series terms sit underneath that picture and cannot be thinned away. The semiconductor contributes a quantum capacitance set by its density of states, and the electrode contributes one too, because a real conductor screens an applied field over a finite depth rather than at a mathematical plane. Both appear in series with the oxide, so measured capacitance always lands below the nominal value and the gap widens as the oxide shrinks.
items.deeper_md:
The dielectric is grown out of the gate. A room-temperature SF₆/Ar plasma (10 sccm SF₆, 5 sccm Ar, 50 mTorr, 50 W) converts the Bi₂Se₃ surface to amorphous BiF₃, and the conversion self-limits at 40–43 nm after 20–25 s. Density-functional calculations put a gap-opened interface immediately under the BiF₃ and a reconstructed, gap-closed Bi₂Se₃-derived layer one step below it, with a localised dipole between them.

The electrical result cuts both ways. Thickness-normalised effective permittivity for the pair is ≈15–16 against ≈28.65 for BiF₃ alone — a capacitance penalty, with an extracted effective quantum capacitance near 2.52 µF/cm². Yet the MoS₂ transistors show subthreshold swing ≈65 mV/dec versus ≈83 for BiF₃-only controls, drain-induced barrier lowering of ≈12 mV/V versus ≈87, negligible hysteresis, and on/off above 10⁶ against ≈10⁵.

The authors are the ones raising the caveats. They decline to assign the improvement causally to the finite quantum capacitance, calling it an independent electrostatic signature rather than the mechanism, and they refuse to claim a topological invariant for the buried state. And at 40 nm of a permittivity-15 film this is a research stack, not an equivalent-oxide-thickness contender.

glossary.definition: Drain-induced barrier lowering: how many millivolts the threshold voltage shifts per volt applied to the drain. It measures the drain stealing electrostatic control of the channel from the gate.
The gate voltage needed to change drain current tenfold below threshold; room temperature puts a floor near 60 mV/decade, so 65 means the gate is close to full control.
The capacitance arising because adding charge to a material with a finite density of states shifts its Fermi level; it sits in series with the oxide and cannot be removed by thinning the oxide.

A material that is insulating in its bulk but carries conducting states on its surface, protected by the symmetry of its band structure — here it is the gate electrode, and its surface is what gets converted.

items.fab_angle: Turning a surface into its own dielectric with a short room-temperature plasma is a step a teaching cleanroom's reactive-ion etcher can run, and the self-limiting depth is the useful part: the film stops thickening because fluorine stops penetrating, so thickness is set by chemistry and ion range rather than by a timed recipe that has to be requalified every session.

items.title: Swap the Schottky gate for a p-n junction and AlGaN blocks 2.5 kV
items.dek: Jonathan Pratt and ten co-authors put a room-temperature sputtered film of p-type chromium oxide where an aluminium-gallium-nitride power transistor normally carries a plain metal gate, and report devices blocking more than 2,500 volts at 11.2 milliohm-square-centimetres of on-resistance.
items.why_it_matters: A metal-on-semiconductor gate on high-aluminium AlGaN leaks and concentrates the field at the gate edge, so the device breaks down well below what the material itself can stand. A p-n junction gate depletes the channel from the semiconductor side instead, which both moves the threshold positive — by 1.63 V here — and spreads the field that would otherwise pile up at one corner. Doing it with a sputtered oxide at room temperature is the part that changes what is buildable: AlGaN refuses p-type dopants outright, and the alternative p-layers need epitaxy that a finished channel's thermal budget will not always pay for.
items.background_md: Aluminium gallium nitride withstands a higher electric field the more aluminium it contains, which is why it is pushed past silicon carbide and gallium nitride for high-voltage switching and radio-frequency power. The crystal will not accept p-type dopants — acceptor levels sit too deep to ionise at room temperature — and heavy aluminium content makes n-type contacts resistive too. Mobile charge in the channel therefore comes from polarisation: grading the aluminium fraction through the layer leaves a fixed bound charge that an electron sheet must balance. Any p-type region has to be supplied by a different material placed on top.
items.deeper_md:
The numbers, all from the preprint's abstract. Reverse-graded n-AlGaN contact layers bring contact resistance to 0.56 Ω·mm. The Cr₂O₃ gate turns on above 3.5 V and shifts threshold +1.63 V against a Schottky reference, with maximum current 590 mA/mm and an on/off ratio of 3×10⁷. At a 9.55 µm gate-drain spacing, breakdown exceeds 2.5 kV with 11.2 mΩ·cm² specific on-resistance and an average breakdown field above 2.5 MV/cm; shorter gate-drain devices reach up to 5.3 MV/cm at 0.28 mΩ·cm².

Those last two sentences describe different devices, and the difference is the whole trade. The same group previously reported 5.3 MV/cm average breakdown field using dielectrics and field plates, but at breakdown voltages above 260 V with 342 mA/mm and a 9.1 GHz cutoff — high field over a short gap. Stretching the gap to 9.55 µm buys the kilovolts and gives most of the field back.

What is missing is time. The abstract reports no gate-bias stress, no high-temperature reverse-bias result and no current-dispersion measurement, and a sputtered oxide sitting on a polarisation-doped channel is exactly where trapping would show up. The superlatives attached to the contact resistance and the breakdown voltage are the authors' own, on a preprint nobody has reviewed.

glossary.definition: Grading the aluminium fraction through an AlGaN layer leaves an unbalanced fixed charge from the crystal's spontaneous and piezoelectric polarisation, which pulls in a mobile carrier sheet without any dopant atoms being added.
Resistance of a contact normalised to its width, because current enters a lateral device along an edge rather than through an area; 0.56 Ω·mm is low for high-aluminium AlGaN.
On-state resistance multiplied by active area. Normalising by area is what lets devices of different size be compared, and it is the denominator of every power-device figure of merit.

A gate made by putting metal directly on the semiconductor, controlling the channel through the depletion region of that metal–semiconductor barrier; simple to build, and it leaks once the barrier is stressed.

items.fab_angle: A p-layer that arrives from a sputter target at room temperature costs no thermal budget and needs no epitaxy reactor, which puts p-n junction gates inside reach of a lab that owns a sputterer and nothing III-V. The trade a teaching lab would feel first is plasma damage to the surface it is trying to form a junction with — measurable on a plain diode as ideality factor and reverse leakage, before any transistor is built.

items.title: Nineteen students' cell library beats the vendor's by 35% in area
items.dek: Nineteen master's students at ETH Zurich drew, laid out and characterised their own standard-cell library — the few hundred small logic blocks a synthesis tool assembles a digital chip out of — on IHP's open-source 130-nanometre process, and released all 220 cells.
items.why_it_matters: Row height is the parameter that decides digital density, and it is fixed before a single line of RTL is synthesised: fewer routing tracks per row means a shorter cell, more rows on the same die, and shorter wires between them. Dropping from the vendor library's 3.78 µm to 3.36 µm gives an 8×8 matrix-vector multiplier 35% less cell area and 39% less energy, at a clock period 3% longer. None of that is visible in a node name, and it is a trade only somebody with the layout rules and the characterisation flow can make — which, with an open process design kit, is now a university course rather than a vendor.
items.background_md: Digital chips are not drawn transistor by transistor. A library of a few hundred pre-drawn cells — inverters, NANDs, flip-flops, each in several drive strengths — is laid out once and characterised into timing and power tables, after which synthesis and place-and-route reason only in terms of those cells. Every cell in a library shares one row height, quoted in routing tracks, because rows have to abut and power rails have to line up. That height sets how much area a given function costs and how far its signals travel, so the library, not the process by itself, fixes the density a design can reach.
items.deeper_md:
EZ130 8T is eight tracks on a 0.42 µm routing grid, so 3.36 µm tall, against IHP's own sg13g2 cells at 3.78 µm with integrated well taps. Metal 1 routes inside the cells at its 0.16 µm minimum width. The 220 cells are characterised with Cadence Liberate at three corners — TT 1.20 V/25 °C, FF 1.32 V/−40 °C, SS 1.08 V/125 °C — and signed off with Siemens Calibre for physical verification and QuestaSim for function. On the 8×8 matrix-vector multiplier the clock period lands at 5.05 ns against 4.89 ns, and the normalised area×time×energy product at 0.41.

Two things to hold against the area number. A shorter row carries less routing resource, so a design with heavier interconnect than a multiplier can hand the area back as congestion; one benchmark does not settle that. And the drive-strength ladder is thin — mostly X1 and X2, with buffers and inverters going to X64 — which limits what a timing optimiser can do and is a plausible source of the 3% period loss. The release page calls the library silicon-validated; measured silicon data is not in the paper.

glossary.definition: One pitch of the lowest routing metal. Quoting a library as 8T means its cells are eight such pitches tall, which is the single number that most determines how dense a synthesised block comes out.

A pre-drawn, pre-characterised layout of one small logic function with fixed height and fixed power-rail positions, so that an automated tool can place thousands of them in abutting rows without redrawing transistors.

The foundry's description of what it will build: device models, design-rule checks, layer definitions and extraction decks. Without one, a layout cannot be verified or simulated against the process that will make it.
Simulating every cell across input slews, output loads and process corners to produce the delay and power tables that static timing analysis reads; it is why adding one cell to a library is not free.

items.fab_angle: This is the design half of a vertically integrated flow made openable: SG13G2 is an Apache-2.0 PDK with device models, DRC/LVS decks and GDS, and EZ130 8T is now a second cell library to synthesise against on the same rules. A club designing a custom IC can compare two libraries on its own netlist and see the row-height trade in its own numbers rather than reading about it.

items.title: Fourteen eviction policies, and plain LRU is still the one to use
items.dek: Yiyu Liu, Minlan Yu and Juncheng Yang replayed production request traces from two language-model serving companies against 14 cache-eviction algorithms, and found that none of the sophisticated ones beats plain least-recently-used at choosing which cached prompt prefixes to discard.
items.why_it_matters: The reason is structural rather than a tuning accident, which is what makes it useful: agent sessions come back on a regular cadence, so how recently a prefix was touched predicts reuse better than how often it was touched, and the frequency-based policies collapse outright. That closes off the obvious direction for improvement and opens a different one. A large gap to the offline optimum remains, and the paper argues it lives in the cost of a miss rather than the count of them — attention work grows with sequence length, so two policies with identical hit ratios can leave very different amounts of prefill to redo.
items.background_md: Answering a prompt has two phases with different bottlenecks. Prefill pushes the whole input through the model once and is compute-bound; decode then emits one token at a time and is memory-bound. A server that has already prefilled some text can keep the key and value tensors it produced and skip that work when the next request begins with the same tokens, which is why serving stacks index cached prefixes by token prefix. That cache competes for the same high-bandwidth memory the weights and the running batch need, so something must be evicted, and the eviction policy decides how much prefill is actually avoided.
items.deeper_md:
The traces are the contribution as much as the result: FreeInference, 327.5K requests and 10.5B tokens over 7 days, agent-heavy; and Chutes, 515.8K requests and 9.7B tokens over 130.9 days, mixing multi-turn chat with agent sessions. Against those, 14 policies spanning recency (LRU), quick demotion (ARC, SIEVE, S3-FIFO, S4-FIFO, LIRS), analytic modelling (LHD), frequency (LFU, W-TinyLFU), learned (LeCaR, LRB, 3LCache) and domain-specific designs, plus Belady's offline optimum as the ceiling. At a 24 GiB cache the sophisticated policies come out very similar to LRU or slightly worse, while the distance to Belady stays large.

The proposed metric is a compute-savings ratio that weights each hit by the prefill cost it avoided, and the recommended design is LRU plus three narrow additions: quick demotion for one-hit prefixes, compute-aware partial eviction for expensive misses, and eviction granularity that varies with capacity.

Two honest limits. Quick demotion pays only when one-hit prompts dominate traffic, and those are small in footprint next to multi-turn sessions. And this is a trace-driven simulation of two operators; the authors note the conclusions can move with a different attention design, a different load balancer, or SSD offload behind the HBM tier. Worth noting who is reporting it: Juncheng Yang is an author of S3-FIFO, one of the policies shown not to transfer.

glossary.definition: The key and value tensors attention computed for every token already processed. Keeping them is what lets a model continue a sequence without recomputing it, and they are what the prefix cache stores.
The first pass that processes an entire prompt at once before any output token is generated; it is compute-bound and its cost grows faster than linearly with prompt length because of attention.

The eviction policy that discards whatever will be needed furthest in the future. It requires knowing the future, so it is unimplementable and used only as the ceiling any real policy is measured against.
Evicting newly admitted objects fast unless they are used again, on the theory that most objects are never reused; it is the idea behind the FIFO-based policies this study finds do not help here.

items.title: Add two prompts together and the model answers both at once
items.dek: Pavel Tikhonov and eight co-authors report that adding the embeddings of two unrelated texts and feeding the sum to a language model produces a next-token distribution close to the mixture of what each text would have produced on its own.
items.why_it_matters: A transformer is assembled from softmax attention, layer normalisation and GELU activations, none of which is linear, so two inputs passing through without scrambling each other says the network behaves more like an additive channel than its parts suggest. The direction of the trend is the awkward part: the effect is strongest at the earliest training checkpoints and weakens as pretraining continues, so it is a property of the architecture that training spends capacity eroding rather than something the model learns. Every technique that reads or steers a model by adding and subtracting activation directions is standing on the same linearity, and this measures how much of it there is.
items.background_md: A transformer carries one running vector per token — the residual stream — and each attention block and feed-forward block adds its output into that vector rather than replacing it. That additive skeleton is why so much interpretability work treats directions in the stream as objects you can add, subtract and project: steering vectors, the logit lens, and sparse dictionaries of features all assume the model is close to linear wherever they intervene. The blocks themselves are not linear, so how far the assumption holds is an empirical question with no theorem behind it, and it is rarely measured end to end.
items.deeper_md:
Tested across Pythia 160M–6.9B, Qwen 0.5B–3B, Llama 1B–8B, OLMo and Gemma, on TinyStories and FineWeb. For base models the KL divergence between the mixed output and the ideal linear mixture runs 0.91–2.16, and a superposition approximation ratio stays below 1 — closer to the ideal mixture than to an unrelated context, which is the control that matters. Hidden-state additivity error rises monotonically over the Pythia training checkpoints.

The effect can be put back. Self-distillation against a frozen copy of the model, using about 0.025% of the original pretraining data and 114–132 GPU-hours on Pythia-2.8B, takes KL from 1.86 to 0.27 and the approximation ratio from 0.42 to 0.06. A joint contrastive decoder then pulls two continuations out of one forward pass: mean LAMBADA accuracy 0.110–0.430 on superposed inputs after fine-tuning, against 0.065–0.182 before, with token overlap between the two streams at a Jaccard of 0.061–0.067.

The gap is the honest number. Single-stream baselines score 0.225–0.643 on the same task, so two answers from one pass are still much worse than two passes. The authors attribute the residual gap to a geometric obstruction rather than to incomplete optimisation, and they test only contexts of 128 tokens or fewer, largely in English.

glossary.definition: The per-token vector that runs the depth of a transformer; every block writes its output into it by addition, which is what makes directions in it behave like things that can be summed.
A measure, in nats, of how far one probability distribution is from another. Here it scores the gap between the model's output on a summed input and the exact average of its two separate outputs.
A word-prediction benchmark whose final word is guessable from a whole passage but not from the last sentence, so it scores whether a model is actually using long-range context.
Fine-tuning a model against the outputs of a frozen copy of itself rather than against labels; here the targets are the two single-stream distributions the superposed input is supposed to reproduce.

foundations.subtitle: The one measurement a new resist owes you, how to take it on a bench, and what γ does and does not predict.
foundations.tldr: Coat a wafer, expose a row of identical squares at steadily increasing doses, develop them all together, and measure how much resist is left on each. Plot that against the logarithm of dose and you get the contrast curve: a plateau, a knee, a steep fall, and a dose at which the resist is gone. Two numbers come out — the clearing dose, which sets your exposure time, and the slope, which sets how sharp an edge the resist can make out of a blurry projected image.

sections.heading: The measurement, and why it is the first one you take
sections.body_md:
You have a new bottle of resist, or an old bottle after a hot summer, or a projector whose LED has aged. You do not yet know what exposure to use, and guessing costs a wafer per guess. The contrast curve answers it in one run.

The recipe is deliberately boring. Spin a film at a fixed speed, soft bake it at a fixed time and temperature, then expose a series of large identical pads — hundreds of micrometres across, so that no optical resolution effect intrudes — at doses stepped in a geometric series, because the useful axis is logarithmic. Develop every pad in the same beaker at the same time, at a temperature you actually measured. Then measure remaining film thickness on each pad and normalise it to the starting thickness.

Everything here is a control variable. If develop time drifts between pads, the curve you measure is a curve of your patience, not of the resist.

sections.heading: Reading the plot: two numbers, and the slope is the important one
sections.body_md:
For a positive resist, the normalised thickness sits near 1 at low dose, breaks downward at some dose, and hits zero at a higher one. Call the break D₀ and the clearing point D₁₀₀, as Kirchauer's lithography thesis does. Contrast is defined as the reciprocal of the log of their ratio:

`γ = 1 / log₁₀(D₁₀₀ / D₀)`

That is just the slope of the falling segment on a log-dose axis, written so that a steeper fall is a bigger number. Kirchauer gives typical values of γ between 2 and 3, which means D₁₀₀ sits only about 2.2 to 3.2 times above D₀ — a representative pair being D₀ of 50 mJ/cm² or below and D₁₀₀ of 150 mJ/cm² or above.

Check which dose a given figure or datasheet means before you compare two of them. The subscripts are not standardised across textbooks, tool vendors and resist suppliers, and a number quoted without its definition is not a number.

sections.heading: Why a steep slope buys resolution you did not pay the optics for
sections.body_md:
The projected image is not a step function. An objective of finite numerical aperture hands the resist a smooth intensity profile that slopes across the intended edge over some distance, and that distance does not shrink because you want it to. The resist's job is to turn that gradient into a binary stencil.

Here is the leverage. Consider the region where intensity crosses the clearing dose. With γ = 2, a factor of 3.2 in dose separates full thickness from no thickness, so every part of the image whose intensity lies inside that band develops to some intermediate thickness — a sloped, blurry sidewall. Push γ up and that band narrows: at γ = 5 the same transition happens over a factor of 1.6 in dose, so a much smaller slice of the image is ambiguous and the printed edge lands closer to where the intensity crossed threshold.

Kirchauer makes the same point in the language of the Rayleigh equation: a higher-contrast resist lowers the achievable k₁, which is the dimensionless factor that says how much of the optics' theoretical resolution the process actually gets.

sections.heading: Dose-to-clear is a property of a process, not of a bottle
sections.body_md:
The clearing dose moves when almost anything moves. Thicker film means more material to bleach and more absorption on the way down, so dose rises with thickness. Stronger developer or a longer soak removes partially exposed resist that a weaker one would leave, which shifts the curve left and usually flattens it. Substrate reflectivity injects a standing wave that makes the number depend on what is underneath. Soft bake decides how much solvent is left in the film, and solvent changes both the dissolution rate and the photochemistry.

This is why the number is only meaningful alongside a recipe. Hacker Fab's published procedure for its maskless stepper pins every one of those: AZ P4210 spun at 4000 rpm for 30 s, soft baked at 100 °C for 90 s, exposed for 8 s, developed in AZ 400K diluted 3:1 with deionised water for 60 s at 20 °C with agitation. Change the dilution to 1:4, as the resist supplier's own product page suggests for the thinner P4110, and the exposure time you carefully calibrated is wrong.

sections.heading: The same resist, a different tool, a different curve
sections.body_md:
Contrast curves are not transferable across exposure sources, because the dose that matters is absorbed dose and absorption depends on how the photons or electrons deposit energy.

Compare two ends of the range. The Hacker Fab stepper images with a 410 nm near-UV LED through a 10×, 0.25 NA objective, giving a Rayleigh-limited feature size near 1 µm and about 2 µm in practice, over a projected field of roughly 1.04 mm × 0.58 mm; its exposures run for seconds. At the other end, Fallica and colleagues measured ZEP520A and mr-PosEBR under extreme-ultraviolet interference lithography and found both to clear at under 12 mJ/cm², resolving 25 nm half-pitch lines with sidewall roughness below 6 nm — and the same resists behave differently again under an electron beam, where energy arrives by electron scattering rather than by photon absorption.

A resist that is fast at one wavelength can be slow or insensitive at another. The curve belongs to the pairing.

sections.heading: What γ will not tell you
sections.body_md:
Contrast is a large-area, bulk measurement, and three things escape it.

It says nothing about edge roughness. Your pads are hundreds of micrometres wide; roughness is a nanometre-scale statistical property of a line edge, driven at short wavelengths by how few photons and how few acid molecules land in a small volume. A resist can have excellent γ and unusable line-edge roughness.

It is not a single number either. Contrast is the local slope, so it depends on where on the curve you are working; a dose chosen at the steepest part of the fall gives more exposure latitude than the same nominal γ used near the toe.

And it does not include dark erosion — the thickness a positive resist loses at zero dose, from development attacking unexposed material. If your plateau sits at 0.9 rather than 1.0, you are losing a tenth of your etch mask before you have printed anything, and no amount of contrast fixes it.
sections.deeper_md: Two refinements worth knowing once the basic curve is in hand. First, the thickness-versus-dose curve and the linewidth-versus-dose curve are different measurements with different uses: the first is what this piece describes, and the second — a CD-versus-dose sweep on an actual pattern — is what sets the exposure latitude you will quote in a process window. Fallica and co-workers use the lumped parameter model precisely to connect them, extracting dose-to-clear and lithographic contrast and then predicting critical dimension against dose for a given tool. Second, for chemically amplified resists the notion of a single exposure dose is already an approximation, because the post-exposure bake diffuses photoacid and the effective dose depends on bake time and temperature as well as on photons delivered. Reporting a clearing dose for such a resist without its bake is the same error as reporting it without its develop time.

glossary.definition: Energy delivered per unit area of the resist surface: intensity multiplied by exposure time. On a stepper with a fixed lamp it is set by time alone, which is why contrast experiments are usually run as time series.

The dose at which a positive resist film is completely removed by development, written D₁₀₀ in the convention used here. It is the practical anchor for choosing an exposure, and it depends on film thickness, developer and development time.

The reciprocal of the base-ten logarithm of the ratio of clearing dose to the dose at which thickness first drops: γ = 1/log₁₀(D₁₀₀/D₀). It is the slope of the falling part of the contrast curve, and a larger value means a sharper conversion from intensity gradient to binary stencil.

Loss of resist thickness in regions that received no exposure, caused by the developer slowly attacking unexposed material. It shows up as a plateau below 1.0 at the left of the curve and it eats etch margin.

The dimensionless prefactor in the Rayleigh resolution equation, half-pitch = k₁λ/NA. It bundles everything that is not wavelength or numerical aperture — illumination, mask enhancement, and resist contrast — into one number, and lowering it is how a process beats its optics.

The bake immediately after spin coating that drives solvent out of the film. It sets residual solvent content, which changes both dissolution rate and photospeed, so it is one of the variables a contrast curve is only valid at.

The sine of the half-angle of light an objective can collect or project, times the refractive index of the medium. It sets both the sharpness of the projected image and, inversely squared, the depth of focus.

foundations.try_this: Run the curve on the club's own stepper this week. Spin one chip of AZ P4210 at 4000 rpm for 30 s and soft bake at 100 °C for 90 s per the Hacker Fab SOP, then expose a row of eight 200 µm squares at 1, 1.5, 2.3, 3.4, 5.1, 7.6, 11.4 and 17 seconds — a geometric series bracketing the SOP's 8 s — and develop all eight together in 3:1 AZ 400K for exactly 60 s. Under the microscope, record the shortest exposure at which a square is completely clear to bare substrate: that is your dose-to-clear in seconds, and bracketing it to ±10% is already a usable result. If you can get a thickness reading on each square, normalise to the unexposed film and plot against log time; the slope of the falling segment is γ, and comparing it against Kirchauer's typical range of 2–3 tells you whether the resist on the shelf is still healthy.
